newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks little moved by Big Bang,await detail.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks little moved by Big Bang,await detail.

text.p: A government panel's financial reform proposals for Japan's securities industry had little direct impact on Tokyo stocks on Friday, but most market participants approved of the plans for change.
When hints of the reforms were first unveiled earlier in the year, Tokyo stocks, plagued by worries over the banking sector, responded favourably, rising nearly four percent.
"The supply/demand situation of the stock market is very good right now," one trader at a foreign brokerage said. "If stocks were still feeble, they may have reacted more."
The Nikkei benchmark ended 36.11 points or 0.18 percent lower at 20,528.35 on Friday.
"The blueprints were announced today and there is still much room for fine-tuning," said Yamaichi Securities general manager Katsumichi Shimizu.
"Stocks may react more strongly once issues concerning the abolishment of the securities transaction tax and the issue over the capital gains tax are clearer," he added.
The Securities and Exchange Council, which is advising the finance minister on the government's "Big Bang" deregulation, has urged the scrapping of the taxes, but without an exact time-frame.
In April 1996, Japan temporarily cut the tax on securities transactions to 0.21 percent from 0.3 percent, although the reduction will lapse in March 1998 unless steps are taken to extend it.
Other proposals included calls for liberalisation of stock brokerage commissions, to be completed by the end of 1999, and the opening up of the securities business to new participants.
"The increased competition will be hard for brokerages, but if business becomes more competitive the quality of the industry will improve," Mitsuru Hayashino, Sanyo Securities general manager, said.

"Investors will benefit greatly from the reforms as they will have a wider choice of business partners to choose from and if trade is easier to do, more investors, especially private investors may be encouraged to invest in the stock market." -- Masako Iijima, Tokyo Equities Desk +81-3-3432-9052
